segments.text: Last chapter bought two signs for a count of ten. This chapter buys five, for a count of ten that Japanese runs beside the one you already have.
ひ — hi.

One stroke, and the KanjiVG stroke data for this sign holds exactly one path: start high on the left, run a short way to the right, then sweep down and far to the left in a long shallow curve and finish by turning up. The pen does not lift once.
Compare ろ, which you wrote five lessons ago: also one stroke, but ろ closes its loop and ひ never closes at all.
Trace ひ (hi) once and copy it once, without lifting.
Hide it; write it after ten seconds.
Write ろ and ひ (hi) side by side: one closes, one does not.
How many strokes? (One.)
Source: Unicode Hiragana chart; stroke count and order per KanjiVG.

feedback.correct: Right: one stroke, and it stays open.

segments.text: ひとつ (hitotsu) — hi-to-tsu — one thing.
Three beats, three signs: ひ (hi) from last lesson, と and つ long since yours.
You already have a word for one. It is いち, and it is borrowed. ひとつ (hitotsu) is the word Japanese had before it borrowed anything, and the two are not interchangeable:

utterances: word: いち. what it is for: the number itself — one, counting aloud, a house number.
word: ひとつ (hitotsu). what it is for: one thing — a thing you are pointing at.

segments.text: Wiktionary's usage note for ひとつ (hitotsu) is one sentence and it is the sentence this chapter turns on: it is used when the items counted have no specific counter category. Hold that. It will be the whole of the next chapter.
Write ひとつ. Say ichi, then hitotsu, and hear that they share nothing — not a beat, not a sound.
Which of the two words is the borrowed one? (いち.)
Sources: Wiktionary: hitotsu.

segments.prompt: You are pointing at one apple. Do you say ichi or hitotsu?
acceptedResponses: hitotsu, because it is a thing

feedback.correct: ichi is the number; hitotsu is one thing.
feedback.incorrect: One is for counting aloud, the other for a thing in front of you.

segments.text: いちど is worth stopping on. Its own lesson said do counts an occurrence — which is to say いちど is a number with a counter behind it, and you have been saying it since chapter nine without anyone calling it that. Two chapters from now that sentence is the whole point.
ふ — fu.

Four separate strokes, in this order, as KanjiVG records them: a short tick at the top; then the body, starting below it and curving down and to the left; then a small mark low on the left; then a small mark low on the right.
Everything this book has taught you so far has been one, two or three strokes. This is the first sign with four, and the last two are easy to run together by accident. They are separate.
Trace ふ (fu) once, counting the four lifts aloud.
Copy it once; hide it; write it again.
Check only one thing: are the bottom two marks separate?
How many strokes? (Four.)
Source: Unicode Hiragana chart; stroke count and order per KanjiVG.

feedback.correct: Four: tick, body, left mark, right mark.

segments.text: ふたつ (futatsu) — fu-ta-tsu — two things.
Three signs, and the only new one arrived last lesson.

Now hear the two words together: ひとつ (hitotsu), ふたつ (futatsu). Both end in つ, and the part in front changes — hito-, futa-. That つ is not decoration. It is the piece doing the counting, and every word in this chapter but the last one carries it.
に is two. ふたつ (futatsu) is two things. Same relation as いち and ひとつ (hitotsu), and again the two words share nothing at all.
Write ふたつ. Say the pair: hitotsu, futatsu. Then say ichi, ni straight after, and hear two different counts running side by side.
What does the つ do? (It counts.)
Sources: Wiktionary: futatsu.

segments.text: みっつ (mittsu) — mi-t-tsu — three things.
Every sign is already yours: み, the small っ, and つ.
The small っ is the sign you met in ゆっくり: it holds the mouth shut for one beat. みっつ (mittsu) is three beats, and the middle one is silence.
さん is three. みっつ (mittsu) is three things.
Write みっつ. Say the run so far, slowly: hitotsu, futatsu, mittsu. Stop on the silent beat in the third one.
How many signs did this word cost? (None — all three were yours.)
Sources: Wiktionary: mittsu.

segments.text: よっつ (yottsu) — yo-t-tsu — four things.
No new sign. よ, the small っ, つ.

blocks.title: Grammar Lens — the seam, from the other side

segments.text: Chapter fourteen taught よん and said something that was left hanging: that split is coming back; it is the same seam the counters run along. Here it is.

よん is a native word standing inside the borrowed count. よっつ (yottsu) is that same native word in the count it belongs to. They begin with the same beat, and that is not an accident — it is one word appearing twice:

utterances: number: one. borrowed: いち. native: ひと-.
number: two. borrowed: に. native: ふた-.
number: three. borrowed: さん. native: み-.
number: four. borrowed: shi. native: よ-.

segments.text: Every other line of the borrowed column is genuinely borrowed. At four, the native word came across into the borrowed count and stayed — which is why the number you actually say for four is よん and not shi. That is what chapter fourteen was pointing at, and you can now see both halves of it at once.
Write よっつ. Say yon, then yottsu, and hear the shared beat. Then say shi and hear that it has none.
Which two words share a beat? (よん and よっつ (yottsu).)
Sources: Wiktionary: yottsu.

segments.prompt: Which word in the borrowed count is really a native word, and which word in this chapter shows where it came from?
acceptedResponses: yon is the native word inside the borrowed count; yottsu is it in its own count

feedback.correct: One word, standing in two counts.
feedback.incorrect: Listen to the first beat of yon and of yottsu.

segments.text: いつつ (itsutsu) — i-tsu-tsu — five things.
Three signs, and two of them are the same one. い, つ, つ.

A warning worth one sentence: いつつ (itsutsu) opens on the same beat as いち, and the two have nothing to do with each other. ご is five; いつつ (itsutsu) is five things; いち is one. The ear will try to pair the wrong two.
Write いつつ. Say ichi and itsutsu back to back, then go and itsutsu, and fix which pair actually means the same number.
Which number does いつつ (itsutsu) NOT mean? (One — however it starts.)
Sources: Wiktionary: itsutsu.

segments.prompt: Which borrowed number means the same as itsutsu?

feedback.correct: Five, not one — the opening beat is a trap.
feedback.incorrect: Count the things: itsutsu is five of them.

segments.text: Five words for two signs. ひ and ふ (fu) were bought in the lessons immediately before the words that needed them; みっつ (mittsu), よっつ (yottsu) and いつつ (itsutsu) cost nothing, because every sign in them was already yours.

Two counts of five now run side by side, and they share exactly one thing: at four, よん and よっつ (yottsu) begin with the same beat. Everywhere else the two words have nothing in common — ichi and hitotsu, ni and futatsu, and so on down.
Five more to go, and three more signs.
